concept.name: Volatility term structure
concept.definition: The volatility term structure is the pattern of at-the-money implied volatility across option expiration dates for the same underlying — typically upward sloping in calm markets (contango) and inverted (near-dated vols above far-dated) around known events or in stressed markets.
concept.intuition: It is the market's calendar of anxiety: comparing implied vol by expiry shows when traders expect turbulence — before an earnings date or election, near-dated vols pop above the back months.
concept.mechanics: ATM implied volatilities are extracted per expiry and plotted against time to maturity; known events (earnings, Fed meetings, harvest reports) create localized humps, after which vol typically falls ('vol crush'). The term structure's slope drives calendar-spread economics and the pricing of variance at different horizons, and it mean-reverts because long-dated vols anchor toward long-run averages.
concept.failure_modes: Comparing raw implied vols across expiries without adjusting for time misleads: total variance grows with horizon, so a 'flat' term structure still implies changing per-period volatility. Event humps also make naive contango/backwardation reads ambiguous around catalysts.
concept.misconceptions: An inverted term structure is not necessarily a trading signal to sell front-month vol — the elevation usually prices a specific scheduled event whose realized move may justify it. The term structure describes implied, not expected realized, volatility.
concept.example: With XYZ earnings in 10 days, the 2-week ATM implied vol trades at 45% while 3-month sits at 25%: an inverted term structure concentrated around the event, which typically collapses once the report is out.
